situation:
You are the director of employee relations at LARKSPUR HEALTH SYSTEM, a hospital system with three hospitals and eleven clinics. The chief operating officer (judge) has asked you to meet this afternoon about a medication safety incident on the night shift and about the practice behind it.

Two difficult years cost LARKSPUR its safety rating and two service lines. New leadership rebuilt the system around a single promise repeated in every hallway and every advertisement: the same care at every hour of the day. Volumes have recovered, and that promise is the reason patients give when they are asked why they came back.

Last month a nurse gave a patient another patient's medication after scanning neither the wristband nor the vial. The patient was not harmed. A review found the scanning step is skipped on roughly one shift in five across the system, most often at night, and that units which scan consistently report far fewer medication errors than units that do not.

Nurses say the scanners are slow, fail at the bedside, and pull them away from patients. Enforcing the rule through discipline tells experienced nurses that a report outweighs what they see at the bedside, and the near-miss reporting the review itself depended on would likely fall. Suspending the requirement until the equipment is replaced leaves a step the system's own records tie to fewer errors out of the process for months.

The chief operating officer (judge) wants you to recommend how LARKSPUR should respond to the incident and to the practice behind it, how that decision will be explained to nursing staff and to the board, and where the system's promise figures in the explanation. You will present to the chief operating officer (judge), who will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the chief operating officer (judge) at LARKSPUR HEALTH SYSTEM. Business background is the same as the situation above. The system rebuilt itself on the promise of the same care at every hour, a night shift medication error has exposed a scanning step that is skipped on about one shift in five, and the nursing staff and the records disagree about why.

You have asked the director of employee relations to recommend how the system should respond to the incident and the practice behind it, how the decision will be explained to nursing staff and to the board, and where the system's promise belongs in that explanation.

After the participant has presented, ask these questions:
judgeQuestions: Which option did you decide against, and what would it have cost us to take it?
If we had gone the other way, what would we be dealing with a year from now?
